prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Multifrequency VLBA observations of the final group of ten objects in a sample of FIRST-based compact steep spectrum (CSS) sources are presented. The sample was selected to investigate whether objects of this kind could be relics of radio-loud AGNs switched off at very early stages of their evolution or possibly to indicate intermittent activity. Initial observations were made using MERLIN at 5 GHz. The sources have now been observed with the VLBA at 1.7, 5 and 8.4 GHz in a snapshot mode with phase-referencing. The resulting maps are presented along with unpublished 8.4-GHz VLA images of five sources. Some of the sources discussed here show a complex radio morphology and therefore a complicated past that, in some cases, might indicate intermittent activity. One of the sources studied - 1045+352 - is known as a powerful radio and infrared-luminous broad absorption line (BAL) quasar. It is a young CSS object whose asymmetric two-sided morphology on a scale of several hundred parsecs, extending in two different directions, may suggest intermittent activity. The young age and compact structure of 1045+352 is consistent with the evolution scenario of BAL quasars. It has also been confirmed that the submillimetre flux of 1045+352 can be seriously contaminated by synchrotron emission.

We report multifrequency VLBA observations of the last ten sources in a sample of compact steep spectrum (CSS) objects selected from the FIRST survey. This sample was designed to test whether such sources might represent radio-loud AGNs that shut down during very early evolutionary phases, or whether they may instead point to episodic activity. The first observations were carried out with MERLIN at 5 GHz. The objects have since been observed with the VLBA at 1.7, 5, and 8.4 GHz, using phase-referenced snapshot observations. We present the resulting radio maps, together with previously unpublished VLA images at 8.4 GHz for five of the sources.

Several of the objects examined display intricate radio structures, implying a complex history and, in some cases, possible recurrent activity. One source in the sample, 1045+352, is already identified as a powerful broad absorption line (BAL) quasar with strong radio emission and high infrared luminosity. This object is a young CSS source with an asymmetric, two-sided structure extending over several hundred parsecs in two distinct directions, a configuration that may indicate intermittent activity. Its youth and compactness agree with proposed evolutionary models for BAL quasars. In addition, it has been verified that synchrotron radiation can significantly contaminate the submillimetre flux measured from 1045+352.
outputs.L3:
Multifrequency VLBA observations were carried out for the final ten objects in a sample of compact steep spectrum (CSS) sources selected from the FIRST survey. These observations form part of a broader effort to understand the nature and evolutionary status of compact radio sources, particularly those whose small linear sizes and steep radio spectra suggest that they may represent young stages of radio-source evolution.

The main goal of the study was to determine whether these CSS sources are relics of radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGNs) that switched off at an early stage of their development, or whether they instead provide evidence for intermittent or recurrent nuclear activity. In the first scenario, the compact radio structures would be remnants of a short-lived episode of jet production that ceased before the source could grow into a large-scale radio galaxy. In the second scenario, the observed structures would reflect multiple phases of activity, with older radio components coexisting alongside newly restarted jets.

The sources were initially observed with MERLIN at 5 GHz, providing intermediate-resolution radio images of their compact structures. They were subsequently observed with the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) at 1.7, 5, and 8.4 GHz, allowing their radio morphologies and spectral properties to be studied on milliarcsecond scales. For five of the sources, additional unpublished Very Large Array (VLA) images at 8.4 GHz were also available, offering complementary information on larger-scale emission.

The observations reveal that several of the sources possess complex radio morphologies. Rather than showing simple, symmetric compact double or core-jet structures, some objects display distorted components, multiple emission regions, or asymmetries that point to more complicated evolutionary histories. Such structures may indicate interactions between the radio jets and a dense surrounding medium, changes in jet direction, or repeated episodes of jet activity. These characteristics make intermittent activity a plausible explanation for at least some members of the sample.

One particularly notable object is 1045+352, a young and powerful broad absorption line (BAL) quasar. Its radio structure is asymmetric and two-sided, suggesting that the source has undergone more than one phase of activity. This morphology supports the interpretation that 1045+352 is an intermittently active radio source rather than a simple, continuously expanding young object. In addition, its radio emission may contribute significantly to its observed submillimetre flux through synchrotron radiation, implying that care must be taken when interpreting its submillimetre emission as purely thermal dust emission. Overall, the study shows that compact steep spectrum sources can have diverse and complex histories, and that some may be linked to recurrent AGN activity rather than a single early evolutionary phase.
outputs.L4:
Multifrequency Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) observations, complemented by imaging data from MERLIN and the Very Large Array (VLA), were used to investigate a sample of ten compact steep spectrum (CSS) radio sources selected from the FIRST survey. The main goal of the study was to determine whether these compact, steep-spectrum objects represent genuinely young radio sources, relics of radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGNs) whose central engines have recently switched off, or systems in which the radio activity is intermittent and has restarted after a period of quiescence.

The observations reveal that several of the sources have complex radio morphologies rather than simple, symmetric double structures. Such complexity suggests that their evolutionary histories may be more complicated than a single, uninterrupted phase of radio-source growth. In some cases, distorted structures, asymmetries, multiple components, or evidence for changing jet directions may indicate interactions between the radio plasma and the surrounding interstellar medium, recurrent nuclear activity, or both.

Particular attention is given to the source 1045+352, which is identified as a young broad absorption line (BAL) quasar. Its compact and highly asymmetric radio structure suggests that it is not merely a simple young source expanding uniformly into its environment. Instead, the morphology is consistent with a scenario in which the quasar has undergone intermittent episodes of radio activity, possibly connected with the broader evolutionary phase associated with BAL quasars. The radio structure may therefore provide evidence that BAL quasars can represent an early or transitional stage in the development of radio-loud AGNs.

The study also shows that the submillimetre emission from 1045+352 may be significantly affected by synchrotron radiation from the compact radio source. This is important because submillimetre flux is often used to estimate dust emission and star-formation activity in quasar host galaxies. If synchrotron contamination is strong, then the inferred dust or star-formation contribution may be overestimated. Overall, the results support the idea that at least some compact steep spectrum sources are not simply young versions of large radio galaxies, but may instead reflect recurrent or interrupted AGN activity combined with strong interactions between jets and their environments.
outputs.L5:
Multifrequency observations with the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) provide a powerful way to study compact radio sources in exceptional detail. By observing the same target at several radio frequencies, astronomers can investigate the structure, spectrum, and physical conditions of active galactic nuclei, quasars, and other compact radio emitters. Such observations make it possible to distinguish between flat-spectrum compact cores, steep-spectrum jet components, and regions affected by absorption or synchrotron aging.

The VLBA is especially useful because of its very high angular resolution, achieved through very long baseline interferometry. It can reveal milliarcsecond-scale structures that are not visible in lower-resolution radio surveys. This allows researchers to identify compact cores, trace relativistic jets, measure component motions, and study how radio morphology changes with frequency.

The FIRST survey, conducted at 1.4 GHz with the Very Large Array, is often used as a starting point for selecting radio sources. FIRST provides wide-area coverage with arcsecond-scale resolution, making it valuable for identifying candidate compact or extended radio sources. Sources detected in FIRST can then be followed up with multifrequency VLBA observations to examine their small-scale structure in much greater detail.

Combining FIRST data with multifrequency VLBA imaging helps connect large-scale radio properties with parsec-scale morphology. FIRST can show the overall radio emission and environment of a source, while the VLBA reveals the compact central regions. This combination is important for understanding the evolution of radio galaxies, the nature of compact steep-spectrum sources, and the role of jets in active galactic nuclei.

counterfactuals.output:
We present multifrequency Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) observations of the final ten compact steep spectrum (CSS) sources selected from the Faint Images of the Radio Sky at Twenty Centimeters (FIRST) survey. These observations complete the VLBI imaging of the FIRST-based sample of compact, steep-spectrum radio sources and provide milliarcsecond-scale information on their morphology, spectra, and physical properties. The VLBA data, supplemented by archival and new MERLIN and VLA observations, allow us to trace the radio structure over a broad range of angular scales and to investigate the connection between parsec-scale components and kiloparsec-scale emission.

The sources display a range of compact radio morphologies, including core–jet, asymmetric double, and candidate compact symmetric object structures. Spectral-index information derived from the multifrequency data is used to identify likely core components, distinguish optically thin jet and lobe emission, and assess the effects of synchrotron self-absorption or free–free absorption in the most compact regions. Several objects show evidence for distorted or misaligned radio structures, suggesting interaction between young radio jets and a dense interstellar medium. Particular attention is given to the broad absorption line quasar 1045+352, whose complex and possibly restarted radio morphology supports a scenario in which jet propagation is strongly affected by the surrounding medium and may be linked to nuclear outflow activity.

Our results confirm that FIRST-selected CSS sources are a heterogeneous population dominated by young radio AGN, but with significant source-to-source differences in orientation, environment, and evolutionary stage. The combined VLBA, MERLIN, and VLA imaging demonstrates the importance of multifrequency, multiscale radio observations for identifying compact cores, characterizing jet evolution, and understanding the role of jet–ISM interactions in compact steep spectrum sources.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the findings of a study investigating whether compact steep spectrum radio sources are young/relic AGNs or evidence of intermittent activity, with emphasis on VLBA observations and source 1045+352.
counterfactuals.output:
The study’s main conclusion is that at least some compact steep spectrum (CSS) radio sources are not simply “ordinary young radio galaxies” evolving smoothly into large FR I/FR II systems. VLBA imaging shows that several CSS objects contain structural and spectral evidence for interrupted or restarted jet activity, often combined with strong interaction between the radio jet and a dense interstellar medium.

Key findings:

- **CSS sources are genuinely compact and young in many cases**, with radio structures confined to the inner few kiloparsecs and steep radio spectra typical of compact lobes/jets.
- However, **their morphologies are often too complex for a single, simple young-source scenario**. VLBA images reveal bends, misalignments, asymmetric components, and diffuse steep-spectrum emission that can be interpreted as relic plasma from earlier activity.
- The observations support a picture in which some CSS sources undergo **intermittent AGN activity**: a new jet episode starts before emission from an older cycle has fully faded.
- Jet–ISM interaction is important. Dense gas in the host galaxy can deflect, slow, or disrupt the young jets, producing compact, distorted radio structures.

### Emphasis on 1045+352

Source **1045+352** is a particularly important example. It is a CSS quasar, also classified as a BAL quasar, and VLBA observations show a highly complex parsec-scale radio morphology.

The VLBA data indicate:

- A compact central component interpreted as the **active core or inner jet region**.
- Several surrounding radio components with steep spectra, likely representing **older jet/lobe material**.
- Strong **misalignment between different radio components**, suggesting that the jet direction has changed with time.
- Evidence consistent with a **restarted or precessing jet**, rather than a single straight jet produced in one continuous phase of activity.
- The distorted structure may result from the new jet interacting with a dense circumnuclear medium, possibly connected with merger-driven activity and the BAL outflow.

Thus, 1045+352 is interpreted as a strong candidate for **intermittent/recurrent AGN activity**: a young, currently active jet is embedded within or interacting with relic emission from a previous episode. The source therefore supports the broader idea that some CSS objects are not merely young radio sources, but may represent short-lived, disrupted, or repeatedly restarting phases of radio-loud AGN evolution.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft the introduction-style summary for a paper presenting multifrequency radio maps of ten compact steep spectrum objects observed with VLBA, MERLIN, and unpublished VLA data.
counterfactuals.output:
Compact Steep Spectrum (CSS) radio sources are powerful, sub-galactic radio objects whose small linear sizes and steep high-frequency spectra make them key laboratories for studying the early stages of radio-source evolution and the interaction between young jets and the dense interstellar medium of their host galaxies. Distinguishing between intrinsically young sources and objects confined by their environments requires high-resolution imaging over a broad range of radio frequencies, so that the morphology, spectral-index distribution, and possible signatures of absorption or jet–cloud interaction can be examined in detail.

In this paper we present multifrequency radio maps of a sample of ten CSS objects observed with the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), MERLIN, and previously unpublished Very Large Array (VLA) data. The combination of these instruments provides sensitivity to structures on scales ranging from parsecs to kiloparsecs, allowing us to trace compact cores, jets, lobes, and diffuse extended emission within the same sources. By comparing images at multiple frequencies and angular resolutions, we investigate the structural properties of the sample, identify candidate core components where possible, and derive spatially resolved spectral information across the radio emission.

These observations provide a homogeneous view of the radio morphology of the ten compact sources and help place them within the broader evolutionary sequence linking young CSS and GHz-peaked spectrum sources to larger-scale radio galaxies and quasars. The maps presented here also form a basis for future studies of source ages, jet propagation, environmental confinement, and the role of the ambient medium in shaping the observed radio structures.

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a research-paper abstract on compact steep spectrum sources selected from FIRST, focusing on their radio morphology, possible intermittent AGN activity, and the young BAL quasar 1045+352.
counterfactuals.output:
**Abstract** — We present a study of compact steep spectrum (CSS) radio sources selected from the Faint Images of the Radio Sky at Twenty Centimeters (FIRST) survey, with emphasis on their parsec- to kiloparsec-scale radio morphology and implications for the early evolution of radio-loud active galactic nuclei (AGN). CSS sources are generally interpreted as young radio objects whose jets are still confined within the host galaxy; however, a growing number show complex, distorted, or multi-episodic structures that may indicate intermittent nuclear activity and strong jet–interstellar medium interactions. Using high-resolution radio imaging, we examine morphological signatures such as compact cores, asymmetric lobes, bent jets, misaligned components, and diffuse relic emission. These features suggest that, in some CSS sources, radio activity may proceed in recurrent phases rather than as a single continuous outburst.

Particular attention is given to the young broad absorption line (BAL) quasar **1045+352**, a CSS object exhibiting a compact, complex radio structure. Its morphology is consistent with a recently triggered or restarted radio source in which the jet propagation is affected by a dense and inhomogeneous circumnuclear medium. The coexistence of BAL outflows and compact radio emission supports a scenario in which 1045+352 represents an early evolutionary stage of quasar activity, possibly associated with the clearing of gas and dust from the nuclear region. Evidence for jet bending or disrupted propagation may reflect either strong interaction with the ambient medium or changes in the jet axis between successive episodes of AGN activity.

Overall, FIRST-selected CSS sources provide an important laboratory for investigating the onset of radio-loud AGN activity, the role of intermittent jet production, and the connection between young radio sources, quasar winds, and host-galaxy evolution. The case of 1045+352 highlights the value of combining radio morphology with spectral and absorption-line diagnostics to distinguish between youth, frustration, and recurrent activity in compact radio AGN.
